items.prompt: Why is bone hard but not brittle like a stick of chalk?

options.label: It is made of pure hard mineral
options.feedback: Pure mineral is what makes chalk snap so easily. Bone survives knocks that would split mineral alone in two.

options.label: It is hollow, so it flexes under a knock
options.feedback: A hollow shape does make a bone lighter for its strength, but shape alone would not stop the material itself from shattering.

options.label: It is a hard shell wrapped around soft tissue
options.feedback: Bone is not a rigid crust over something soft — the strength runs through it, not just across its surface.

options.label: It is tough fibres woven through with hard mineral
options.feedback: The fibres give it a little give, the mineral gives it stiffness, and together they resist both bending and shattering.

items.ok_line: One ingredient bends, the other holds firm.
items.ko_line: Ask what stops a hard material from also being a fragile one.
items.exp_text: Pure mineral is stiff but snaps the instant it bends, the way chalk does underfoot. Bone is built from tough collagen fibres running through a mesh, packed with hard mineral crystals along their length. The fibres let the structure flex very slightly and soak up a jolt, while the mineral keeps it stiff enough to carry weight, and swapping either ingredient for more of the other would trade one failure for the opposite one.

items.prompt: Why are many bones hollow or honeycombed inside rather than solid all the way through?

options.label: To let the bone cool down faster
options.feedback: Bone temperature is not something the body needs to manage by shaping its skeleton.

options.label: To leave room for nerves to pass through
options.feedback: Nerves run alongside bone, not through tunnels bored inside it for that purpose.

options.label: So the bone can bend more easily
options.feedback: A hollow bone is not noticeably springier than a solid one of the same size; the hollowing is about weight, not flexibility.

options.label: To carry the same strength for less weight
options.feedback: Material sits mostly at the outer edge, where it resists bending the most, so the core can be hollowed out at little cost to strength.

items.ok_line: Material only where the load actually needs it.
items.ko_line: Think about what an engineer gains by hollowing out a beam rather than casting it solid.
items.exp_text: A solid rod resists bending mainly through the material at its outer edge; the core contributes far less for the weight it adds. Bone follows that same logic on its own: the outer layer is dense and compact, while the inside is either hollow or filled with a lattice of thin honeycombed struts arranged along the lines of greatest stress. The result carries a heavy skeleton's load while sparing the body from hauling around bone it does not need.

items.prompt: What does the soft marrow packed inside many bones actually do?

options.label: It cushions the bone against impact
options.feedback: Cartilage and the bone's own structure absorb impact; marrow sits deep inside, far from any blow.

options.label: It stores air for the lungs to draw on
options.feedback: Bones hold marrow, not air; nothing about breathing routes through the skeleton.

options.label: It produces new blood cells
options.feedback: Marrow is where the body manufactures fresh blood cells to send out into circulation.

options.label: It lubricates the joint at each end of the bone
options.feedback: Joints are lubricated by fluid made in the joint capsule itself, not by anything travelling out from the marrow deep inside.

items.ok_line: The skeleton doubles as a production line.
items.ko_line: Marrow is a soft, living tissue, not a padding or a lubricant.
items.exp_title: A factory hidden in the bone
items.exp_text: Marrow is a soft tissue packed into the hollow core of a bone, and in many bones it is busy round the clock making new blood cells to replace ones that wear out. Those young cells slip out of the marrow and into tiny blood vessels running through the bone, joining the general bloodstream from there. A skeleton works as a frame the body hangs on, and inside it doubles as the place where the blood gets made.

items.prompt: Why do the ends of bones inside a joint have a smooth cap of cartilage rather than meeting as bare bone?

options.label: So the two bones can glide against each other with little friction
options.feedback: A smooth cartilage surface lets the two bone ends slide past each other instead of grinding.

options.label: So the bones can grow longer as the joint moves
options.feedback: Growth in length happens elsewhere in a bone, not because the joint surfaces are rubbing against each other.

options.label: So the joint can carry electrical signals to the brain
options.feedback: Signals about a joint's position travel along nerves nearby, not through the cartilage capping the bone.

options.label: So the bones can be pulled apart and put back together
options.feedback: A healthy joint is not designed to come apart; the cartilage is there for the bones to move against each other while staying joined.

items.ok_line: A slippery cap where two hard surfaces meet.
items.ko_title: Not what the cap is for
items.ko_line: Picture two bare bone ends grinding together with every step.
items.exp_text: Bare bone grinding against bare bone would wear away quickly and grate with every movement, so wherever two bones meet and move against each other, their ends are capped with a smooth layer of cartilage instead. Cartilage has no rough grain and very little friction against itself, so the two capped surfaces glide rather than grind. The joint moves easily because the two hardest parts of it never actually touch.

items.prompt: What is the fluid inside a joint capsule for?

options.label: It dissolves worn cartilage so the joint can reshape itself
options.feedback: The fluid protects cartilage rather than breaking it down; a joint does not reshape itself by dissolving its own lining.

options.label: It lubricates the joint so the cartilage surfaces slide smoothly
options.feedback: A thin coating of this fluid is exactly what lets the two cartilage-capped surfaces glide with so little resistance.

options.label: It carries oxygen to the muscles around the joint
options.feedback: Muscles get their oxygen from blood vessels; the fluid inside the joint capsule stays sealed within the joint itself.

options.label: It hardens over time to lock the joint in place as we age
options.feedback: A working joint stays fluid and mobile; a joint that stiffens and locks is not doing what this fluid is there for.

items.ok_line: A slippery film sealed inside the joint.
items.ko_line: Think of what keeps a hinge from squeaking, not what feeds the muscle around it.
items.exp_text: The membrane lining a joint capsule produces a thick, slippery fluid that coats the cartilage on both bone ends, in much the same way oil coats the metal parts of a hinge. That film lets the cartilage surfaces glide past each other with very little resistance instead of dragging. Squeeze the joint through its range of motion and the fluid spreads with it, keeping the whole surface wetted rather than pooling in one spot.

items.prompt: Why does the spine curve in an S-shape rather than run straight up and down?

options.label: It curves so the spinal cord can stretch when we grow taller
options.feedback: The spinal cord's length is not what the curve is solving; a straight spine could still lengthen as a body grows.

options.label: It curves so the ribs have somewhere to attach
options.feedback: Ribs attach along the spine whatever its shape; the curve is not there to give them an anchor point.

options.label: A curved shape absorbs shock better than a straight column
options.feedback: Each curve flexes a little under a jolt, so the impact reaching the head is softened rather than passed straight through.

options.label: It curves to keep the head from tipping backward
options.feedback: Balancing the head's weight matters, but that is handled by the neck's posture, not by the overall S-shape of the whole spine.

items.ok_line: Curves bend under load instead of transmitting the full jolt.
items.ko_title: Not the reason for the curve
items.ko_line: Compare how a straight rod and a curved spring each react to being jarred from above.
items.exp_text: A straight, rigid column passes a jolt from the ground straight up through itself with almost nothing lost along the way. The spine instead bends through a series of curves, one in the neck, one in the mid-back, one in the lower back, each running the opposite way from the one above it. A jolt travelling up through a curved column flexes each curve slightly rather than slamming straight through it, so the shock arrives at the head far gentler than it left the ground.

items.prompt: Why is the rib cage built from a set of jointed bones rather than one solid plate?

options.label: So broken ribs are easier to replace individually
options.feedback: The skeleton does not repair itself by having damaged parts swapped out; a rib mends where it is, whether or not it sits next to others.

options.label: So the chest can protect the organs inside while still expanding to breathe
options.feedback: Jointed ribs can swing outward and back with every breath while still forming a guard around the heart and lungs.

options.label: So the ribs can be counted more easily during growth
options.feedback: Nothing about the skeleton is shaped for the convenience of counting its parts.

options.label: So sound can pass more easily through the chest
options.feedback: Hearing does not route through the rib cage; the ribs' jointed shape has nothing to do with how sound travels.

items.ok_line: A solid plate could guard the chest, but it could never breathe.
items.ko_line: Ask what a rigid, one-piece chest could never do that a jointed one can.
items.exp_title: A cage that has to move to work
items.exp_text: A single solid plate over the chest would guard the heart and lungs well, but it could never change shape, and breathing depends on the chest changing shape with every breath. Instead, each rib is a curved bone hinged at the spine and joined at the front by a strip of flexible cartilage, so the whole cage can swing outward and back like a set of parallel handles. It shields the organs inside exactly as a solid plate would, while still being able to expand and fall with every breath a plate never could.

items.prompt: Why can a broken bone mend itself back into one solid piece?

options.label: Because bone is a living tissue with its own blood supply
options.feedback: Living cells fed by that blood supply are what build the new tissue that bridges a break.

options.label: Because bone is naturally sticky and the two ends fuse on contact
options.feedback: The two broken ends do not simply stick together; new tissue has to be built to bridge the gap between them.

options.label: Because the surrounding muscle pulls the pieces back into shape
options.feedback: Muscle can hold a limb still, but repairing the break itself is done by the bone's own tissue, not by the muscle around it.

options.label: Because the mineral in bone reforms itself like a crystal regrowing
options.feedback: Bone mineral does not regrow the way a crystal does on its own; living cells have to lay down new tissue first.

items.ok_line: A break heals because something living is doing the mending.
items.ko_line: Ask what a break has that a cracked stone never does.
items.exp_text: Bone is threaded with its own blood vessels and living cells, unlike a piece of stone or wood it might otherwise resemble. When it breaks, blood pools at the gap and the cells there start building a soft bridge of new tissue across it, which is gradually hardened with fresh mineral until it matches the bone on either side. A fracture closes the way it does because bone, however hard it feels, is tissue the body keeps alive and can rebuild.

items.prompt: Why does a skeleton keep changing throughout a person's life instead of being fixed once it is fully formed?

options.label: One kind of cell keeps removing old bone while another lays down new bone
options.feedback: That steady clearing and rebuilding is exactly what keeps a skeleton changing all through life.

options.label: Bone slowly evaporates and is replaced by breathing in fresh mineral
options.feedback: Bone is solid tissue, not something that evaporates; nothing about breathing feeds mineral into the skeleton that way.

options.label: The skeleton is swapped for a new one at intervals through life
options.feedback: There is no wholesale replacement of the skeleton; the same bones are reshaped from within rather than exchanged for others.

options.label: Bones only change shape when they are broken and reset
options.feedback: Reshaping goes on quietly inside bone that has never been broken at all, not only after an injury.

items.ok_line: Two crews at work on the same bone, endlessly.
items.ko_line: The change is constant and internal, not tied to any single event.
items.exp_text: Scattered through bone tissue are cells that dissolve tiny patches of old bone, and close behind them come other cells that fill each cleared patch back in with new tissue. The two kinds of cell work in a steady balance, clearing worn or stressed bone and rebuilding it a little at a time rather than all at once. A skeleton looks like a fixed frame from the outside, but at this small scale it is being quietly taken apart and put back together for as long as a person is alive.

items.prompt: Why is the skull curved into a dome rather than shaped like a flat box?

options.label: The dome shape lets sound waves travel through it more easily
options.feedback: Hearing depends on the ear, not on how sound moves through the skull's shape.

options.label: A domed shape spreads out the force of a blow instead of concentrating it
options.feedback: The curve carries force outward along the bone rather than letting it stay concentrated at the point struck.

options.label: A domed skull is lighter than a flat one would be
options.feedback: Weight is not the reason for the curve; a flat plate covering the same area would not necessarily weigh any more.

options.label: The curve lets the skull flex like a spring to cushion impact
options.feedback: The skull is rigid rather than springy; it protects by spreading force, not by bending under it.

items.ok_title: A shape built to spread force
items.ok_line: A dome shares the load across itself instead of taking it in one place.
items.ko_line: Think about how force travels differently through a curved surface than a flat one.
items.exp_title: A shape that shares the hit
items.exp_text: A flat surface struck at one point takes nearly all of the force right there, with little of it carried away to the rest of the structure. A curved dome does the opposite: the arch of the bone channels force outward along its curve to the rest of the skull, so a single point of impact is shared across a much wider area of bone rather than absorbed by it alone. That spreading is what lets a thin shell of bone guard something as delicate as the brain sitting inside it.
